anatomy.intro: Ming Thing distributes its growth across a collection of irregular clubs.

parts.function: The fleshy blue-green lobe is stem tissue; its uneven outline reflects monstrose growth.
parts.label: Club-shaped stem

parts.function: A small pale cushion is the growing structure from which spines arise.
parts.label: Woolly areole

parts.function: These sparse, stiff projections distinguish the areoles from bare surface bumps.
parts.label: Short dark spines

parts.function: Each rounded lobe tip can extend, adding to the uneven branching silhouette.
parts.label: Growing tip

flowers.text: The underlying species has large, white, night-opening funnels, sometimes tinged purple. NC State specifically notes that Ming Thing rarely flowers, so its changing stem architecture is a more realistic everyday attraction than an expected bloom schedule.

growth.note: Record changes in shape over time; there is no reliable age or height at which this cultivar must flower.

stages.text: The young form starts with a few thick, irregular lobes.
stages.title: Small club

stages.text: Additional growing points produce more knobs and clubs.
stages.title: Sculptural clump

stages.text: The slow-growing cultivar builds a denser outline rather than matching the wild tree.
stages.title: Older mound

habitat.text: The wild species comes from Bolivia through Paraguay into northern Argentina, where it grows in dry shrubland and can become a tree. Ming Thing is a cultivated monstrose form: its miniature club-shaped stems are not the normal outline of a wild Cereus forest. Think of the species range as ancestry, not the cultivar’s own natural habitat.

lookalikes.name: Normal Cereus forbesii
lookalikes.text: The ordinary species forms a ribbed, tree-like cactus; Ming Thing repeatedly interrupts that columnar pattern with clubs and knobs. A single unusually shaped shoot does not prove a different species.

mature.text: NC State describes the cultivar at about 15–30 cm tall and 8–15 cm wide. The tree habit recorded for wild Cereus forbesii should not be substituted for those cultivated expectations.

milestones.text: Joined the collection from Altman Reserve.
milestones.title: Acquired

nameStory.text: The epithet forbesii commemorates a Mr. Forbes, head gardener at Woburn Abbey in England. The cultivated form’s name sits on top of that older botanical dedication.
